children: An Oklahoma judge has acknowledged that a ruling he issued contained fictitious citations generated by artificial intelligence, according to state records, adding to a growing number of cases in which judges have faced scrutiny over AI use.

The judge, Lawrence Wheeler of the District Court of Stephens County, told an investigator with the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation that he used OpenAI’s ChatGPT for research, and that an order he drafted contained two citations to cases that do not exist, according to an August 17 letter from a prosecutor to the state attorney general's office.

Wheeler, who was elected in 2022 and presides over a family law docket, did not immediately respond to a request for comment left with his office in Duncan, Oklahoma. His lawyer, Scott Anderson, said in a statement that “Judge Wheeler and I have no comment on the matter at this time.”

Wheeler's use of AI was included in a judicial misconduct complaint that also alleged that the judge secretly listened to jury deliberations, county district attorney Jason Hicks said in the letter, which was reviewed by Reuters. The Oklahoman newspaper first reported the letter.

The Oklahoma Attorney General’s Office in a statement on Wednesday said it reviewed the allegations but the evidence was insufficient to prosecute. The office said the Oklahoma Supreme Court and another state judicial body have power to discipline judges whether or not there is a criminal violation.

The growing use of AI technology in the courts and at law firms has put new scrutiny on the accuracy of filings and orders, stemming from instances where AI has made up case ​citations or misquoted the law.

Two federal judges last year said the use of AI in their chambers led to errors in two court rulings. A Georgia prosecutor’s use of AI led to erroneous citations appearing in a ruling in a murder case.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

According to the August 17 letter, Hicks recused himself from investigating Wheeler and asked Oklahoma State Attorney General Gentner Drummond to review the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation's report or reassign the inquiry.
Drummond’s office in its statement on Wednesday said its criminal division “thoroughly reviewed” the claims and was not pursuing them further.

The Oklahoma Council on Judicial Complaints in a statement on Wednesday said it cannot comment on or confirm any investigation. The Oklahoma Supreme Court did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
